title: RGB LED colour mixer
content_html:
Materials

  • 1 x Arduino Uno R3 (Nerokas, nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x USB Type-A to Type-B cable (for programming the Uno) (Nerokas, nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x Breadboard, 830 tie-points (Pixel Electronics, pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 1 x RGB LED, common cathode, 5mm (Pixel Electronics, pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 3 x Potentiometers, 10k ohm, linear, with knob (Nerokas, nerokas.co.ke)
  • 3 x Resistors, 220 ohm (colour bands: red-red-brown) (Nerokas, nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 pack x Male-to-male jumper wires (at least 15 wires) (Nerokas, nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x Small flat-head screwdriver or pen (optional, for turning potentiometer knobs if they don't have finger knobs) (Pixel Electronics, pixelelectronics.co.ke)

How It Works

An RGB LED is really three tiny LEDs — one red, one green, one blue — squeezed into a single plastic case. Each colour has its own leg (pin) that we control separately. When we mix different brightness levels of red, green and blue light together, our eyes see a huge range of colours — exactly like a TV or phone screen does.

The Arduino can't make an LED "half bright" in a simple on/off way, because a digital pin only knows two states: HIGH (on) or LOW (off). Instead, it uses a trick called PWM (Pulse Width Modulation). The Arduino flicks the pin on and off very fast — hundreds of times a second — and by changing how long it stays on during each flick, it can make the LED look dimmer or brighter to our eyes. This is what the analogWrite() command does, using a brightness number from 0 (off) to 255 (fully on).

A potentiometer (or "pot") is a knob that acts like an adjustable tap for electricity. As you turn it, it changes how much voltage reaches the Arduino's analog input pin. The Arduino reads this with analogRead(), which gives a number between 0 and 1023. Since our LED brightness only understands numbers 0–255, we use a command called map() to convert the potentiometer's 0–1023 reading into the 0–255 range the LED needs.

Put it all together: turning a knob changes a number, that number becomes an LED brightness, and three knobs together mix red, green and blue into any colour students can imagine — including colours that don't exist as separate LEDs, like purple, orange, or white.

Step-by-Step Instructions

  1. Place the breadboard in front of the group and insert the RGB LED into it. Look closely at the four legs — the longest leg is the common cathode (ground) and always goes to the negative rail. If unsure, check the flat side of the LED casing, which usually sits next to the cathode leg.
  2. Connect the LED's cathode (longest leg) to the breadboard's negative (GND) rail using a jumper wire.
  3. Connect the negative rail on the breadboard to the Arduino's GND pin with a jumper wire.
  4. Take the three remaining LED legs (red, green, blue). Connect each one through its own 220 ohm resistor, then via jumper wire to Arduino pins 9 (Red), 10 (Green), 11 (Blue). These three pins are marked with a "~" symbol on the Uno, meaning they support PWM.
  5. Insert each potentiometer into the breadboard. Each pot has 3 legs: connect one outer leg to 5V, the opposite outer leg to GND, and the middle leg (the "wiper") to an Arduino analog pin — A0 for Red, A1 for Green, A2 for Blue.
  6. Double-check that all three potentiometers share the same 5V and GND rails as the LED circuit — everything on the breadboard should connect back to the Arduino's 5V and GND pins.
  7. Connect the Arduino to a computer with the USB cable, open the Arduino IDE, and paste in the sketch from the "Full Code" section below.
  8. Select the correct board (Arduino Uno) and port from the Tools menu, then click Upload.
  9. Once uploaded, ask students to slowly turn the Red potentiometer. They should observe the red portion of the LED getting brighter or dimmer, changing the overall colour.
  10. Repeat with the Green and Blue potentiometers, observing how each affects the mixed colour on its own.
  11. Challenge students to work together (one knob each) to create a specific target colour, such as purple, yellow, or white.
  12. Open the Arduino IDE's Serial Monitor (set to 9600 baud) to show the live R, G, B numbers changing as the knobs turn — this connects the physical colour to the numbers behind it.

Full Code


// RGB LED Colour Mixer
// Three potentiometers control the brightness of Red, Green, and Blue
// on a common-cathode RGB LED, letting students mix custom colours.

// Pin definitions for the RGB LED (must be PWM-capable, marked with "~")
const int redPin   = 9;
const int greenPin = 10;
const int bluePin  = 11;

// Pin definitions for the three potentiometers (analog input pins)
const int redPot   = A0;
const int greenPot  = A1;
const int bluePot  = A2;

void setup() {
  // Set LED pins as outputs so we can send PWM signals to them
  pinMode(redPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(greenPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(bluePin, OUTPUT);

  // Start Serial communication so we can watch the numbers change live
  Serial.begin(9600);
}

void loop() {
  // Read each potentiometer: returns a number from 0 to 1023
  int redValue   = analogRead(redPot);
  int greenValue = analogRead(greenPot);
  int blueValue  = analogRead(bluePot);

  // Convert each 0-1023 reading into a 0-255 brightness value
  // because analogWrite() only understands 0-255
  int redBrightness   = map(redValue, 0, 1023, 0, 255);
  int greenBrightness = map(greenValue, 0, 1023, 0, 255);
  int blueBrightness  = map(blueValue, 0, 1023, 0, 255);

  // Send the PWM signal to each LED leg to set its brightness
  analogWrite(redPin, redBrightness);
  analogWrite(greenPin, greenBrightness);
  analogWrite(bluePin, blueBrightness);

  // Print the current mix to the Serial Monitor so students can see
  // the numbers behind the colour they are creating
  Serial.print("R: ");
  Serial.print(redBrightness);
  Serial.print("  G: ");
  Serial.print(greenBrightness);
  Serial.print("  B: ");
  Serial.println(blueBrightness); // println moves to a new line after B

  delay(50); // Small pause to keep readings stable and Serial output readable
}

Common Mistakes & Fixes

SymptomLikely CauseFix
LED does not light up at allCommon cathode leg not connected to GND, or LED inserted backwardsCheck the longest leg goes to GND; try rotating the LED 180° if colours seem swapped or missing
Only one or two colours respond to knobsA resistor or jumper wire for one colour leg is loose, missing, or in the wrong breadboard rowTrace each colour leg individually from LED to resistor to Arduino pin; reseat wires firmly
Turning a potentiometer does nothingWiper (middle leg) not connected to the analog pin, or pot's outer legs not connected to 5V/GNDVerify all three legs of the pot: two to power rails, middle one to the analog pin (A0/A1/A2)
LED colour flickers or is unstableLoose breadboard connections or a shared GND rail not fully connectedPress all jumpers firmly into the breadboard; ensure GND rail is continuous and connected to Arduino GND
All colours seem "backwards" (dim when knob turned up, bright when turned down)This is normal pot behaviour depending on wiring orientation — not an errorExplain to students that swapping the two outer wires of the pot reverses the direction; either is fine
Code uploads but Serial Monitor shows nothingBaud rate mismatch or wrong COM port selectedSet Serial Monitor baud rate to 9600 and confirm the correct port is selected in Tools menu

Discussion Questions

  • Why can't the Arduino just tell an LED to be "half bright" using a normal on/off pin?
  • What do you think is happening incredibly fast inside the wire when PWM makes an LED look dim?
  • Why do we need the map() function — what problem does it solve between the potentiometer and the LED?
  • Can you think of a colour you cannot make with just three knobs? Why or why not?
  • Where else in daily life do you think tiny red, green and blue lights are mixed to create colour? (Hint: look at a screen very closely!)

Extension Challenges

  • Easy: Add a fourth potentiometer that controls how fast the LED "breathes" — automatically fading up and down in brightness overall, layered on top of the colour mix.
  • Medium: Modify the code so that when all three potentiometers are turned to their lowest value, the LED blinks red three times as a "warning" that the colour is basically off.
  • Hard: Write code that cycles automatically through a rainbow of colours (without using the potentiometers at all), then have a button press switch between "auto rainbow mode" and "manual knob mixing mode."
